2010.kid: The laptop sends its parcels down a cable to the router. The router’s modem sings them along the old copper phone line as tiny tones, to a box on your street.
2010.nerd: Wired, around 2010: Ethernet from the laptop to a DSL modem-router, which NATs the packets and sends them as VDSL2 tones on the copper phone pair to a DSLAM in the street cabinet, then fibre to the ISP.

describe.kid: A cut-away house shows a desk with a laptop, an old telephone on a little table, and the router. A cable runs from the laptop to the router, and the phone line takes the parcels out to the internet cloud. Requests go out and video comes back.
describe.nerd: The overview follows a wired 2010 home: the laptop, with a star sticker, on Ethernet to a DSL router with two antennas, whose uplink is the copper phone line (VDSL2) it shares with the telephone. Request packets go upstream; video packets return downstream.

laptop.kid: In 2010 the laptop on the desk went online through a cable too. Its request runs down the cable to the router.
laptop.nerd: A 2010 laptop with a gigabit Ethernet port, plugged into one of the modem-router’s 100 Mbit/s LAN ports, so the cable runs at 100: still far faster than the DSL line behind it, often 8–20 Mbit/s down.

router.kid: The router is the front door of your home. It writes your home’s address on the parcel, and its modem sings it down the phone line.
router.nerd: NAT rewrites 192.168.1.40 to the public 203.0.113.7; the built-in VDSL2 modem then sends the frames as DMT tones on the phone pair.

internet.nerd: Access network (VDSL2 from a DSLAM in the street cabinet; most Danish homes in 2010 still had ADSL2+ from the exchange), an aggregation layer (L2 backhaul to the BNG), the ISP’s MPLS core, then either peering at an IXP or paid transit, ending at a CDN cache. Each shaded area is one operator’s network.
